One of the defining attributes of the ATJ process is the potential flexibility of the feedstock supply combined with the maturity of the domestic fuel-ethanol supply chain. Whereas in the case of HEFA or SIP, where the commonly cited feedstocks include only a narrow class of inputs, alcohols can be sourced from a more diverse and broad set of potential resources. Specifically, in addition to the traditional biological approaches for producing alcohol via corn fermentation, additional routes have been developed to produce alcohols from a variety of low- cost waste carbonaceous resources. As one example, engineered microorganisms developed by LanzaTech have been tested and shown to convert raw synthesis gas mixtures (e.g., CO /CO/H ) 2 2 directly into alcohols (LanzaTech 2023). This syngas can be derived from gasification of municipal solid waste streams, electrolysis, or even directly from industrial flue gases (e.g., steel mills). This feedstock flexibility not only serves to increase the potential scalability of ATJ, but in many cases, can also help to lower the input costs and alleviate food versus fuel challenges. Among SAF pathways, ATJ is second only to HEFA in terms of current domestic commercial activity. LanzaJet, a spinoff from LanzaTech, now operates the first and largest commercial- scale ATJ-to-SAF facility at the Georgia Freedom Pines Fuels plant, converting fuel-grade ethanol into SAF. However, despite its technical maturity and promise, ATJ faces several remaining challenges that currently limit large-scale deployment. The most significant barrier is the cost and carbon intensity of alcohol feedstocks. Specifically, while the domestic fuel-grade ethanol market is large, the carbon intensity of conventional fermentation-derived ethanol varies widely and may diminish the potential life cycle benefits of the SAF produced. Fully low-carbon alcohol sources such as second-generation cellulosic ethanol, waste-derived ethanol, or CO - 2 derived alcohols are most sought after; however, their supply remains relatively small and higher in cost. 17 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. 2.1.1.5 Catalytic Hydrothermolysis Catalytic hydrothermolysis is a TRL ~8 pathway and among the latest of the approved SAF pathways, achieving ASTM certification in early 2020. Pioneered by Applied Research Associates under the tradename ReadiJet, CH-derived SAF represents a drop-in ready fuel containing the same molecules with the same performance as petroleum jet fuel, able to meet Jet A, Jet A1, JP-5, and JP-8 fuel specifications without the need for blending with petroleum (Applied Research Associates n.d.). However, blending is currently limited to 50%. The CH conversion process involves the deconstruction of triglyceride-based feedstocks (e.g., seed oils, animal oils, fats, greases) into hydrocarbons via exposure to catalysts in the presence of supercritical or near-supercritical water.
